artwork.title: Head from Keros
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Shonagon, 2023, via Wikimedia Commons · CC0

lessons.title: A face with one feature

n1.text: A white marble head, 27 cm tall, made in the Cyclades islands more than 4,000 years ago. Its face has one carved feature: a long nose.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Stand face to face with it. Count what you can see on the face, then look at what is not there.

q1.text: Why does the face have no eyes or mouth?

b1a.text: It was finished: the face was meant to be painted.

correction.tempting: The face looks blank, as if work stopped.
correction.truth: The carvers shaped the nose and painted eyes, brows and mouth on the smooth marble. The paint has worn away.
correction.evidence: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; Dayton Art Institute.

b1b.text: Yes. Cycladic carvers shaped the nose and painted the rest: dark eyes and brows on the white stone. Which colours this head had is unknown.

b1c.text: Only the nose was ever carved.

correction.tempting: Old marble can be worn smooth.
correction.truth: The other features were painted, not carved, and the paint is what has gone.
correction.evidence: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; Dayton Art Institute.

n2.text: The Louvre calls it a fragment of a statuette. It is only the head: the body it belonged to is lost.

q2.text: Complete figures of this type: how do they hold their arms?

b2a.text: The arms stay low, against the body.

correction.tempting: The head tilts back, as if looking up.
correction.truth: Complete figures of this type fold their arms under the chest.
correction.evidence: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; University of Cambridge.

b2b.text: Nothing reaches out: the arms are folded.

correction.tempting: A figure without a body could have held anything.
correction.truth: Figures of this type fold their arms under the chest, close to the body.
correction.evidence: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; University of Cambridge.

b2c.text: Yes. Most such figures are nude women with the head tilted back, the arms folded under the chest and the feet pointing down.

n3.text: It was made in the Early Bronze Age, around 2600–2400 BC, on islands where nobody yet wrote things down.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Imagine the island workshop: no writing, no labels. Only the stone, and whatever the people who held it knew.

q3.text: What were figures like this made for?

b3a.text: Nobody knows what they were for.

correction.tempting: Many are small enough to hold in one hand.
correction.truth: Their purpose is unknown. Most excavated ones come from graves, and some from settlements.
correction.evidence: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; the Louvre curator Ludovic Laugier (Centre Pompidou, 2023).

b3b.text: Yes. They come from a time without writing, and many were dug up without records. Most excavated ones come from graves; some from settlements.

correction.tempting: The Louvre describes it as a female figure.
correction.truth: Nobody knows whom or what these figures show, or what they were for.
correction.evidence: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; the Louvre curator Ludovic Laugier (Centre Pompidou, 2023).

n4.text: The label says it was found on Keros, a small island now almost empty of people. Keros is famous for the "Keros Hoard": fragments looted in the 20th century.

q4.text: Could this head be part of the looted Keros Hoard?

choices.label: No: the dates rule it out

correction.tempting: The label and the Hoard both name Keros.
correction.truth: The Louvre had this head by 1873. The Hoard was looted and sold in the 20th century.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; University of Cambridge.

b4b.text: Here the dates do settle it.

correction.tempting: So much about these figures is unknown.
correction.truth: The head was in the Louvre by 1873; the Hoard surfaced in the 20th century.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; University of Cambridge.

b4c.text: Yes. Olivier Rayet gave the head to the Louvre in 1873. The Hoard reached the market in the 20th century, long after.

n5.text: In the 20th century, artists such as Brancusi, Modigliani, Picasso and Henry Moore admired Cycladic figures like this one.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Look at the smooth oval again. Can you see why sculptors of the 1900s found it so modern?

q5.text: In 2024 the Louvre lent this head to an exhibition on which sculptor?

b5a.text: Yes. The Centre Pompidou in Paris showed it with Brancusi's work, so visitors could compare the ancient and the modern shapes.

correction.tempting: The head is polished white marble.
correction.truth: The 2024 loan was to the Centre Pompidou's Brancusi exhibition in Paris.

correction.tempting: The head is polished white marble.
correction.truth: The 2024 loan was to the Centre Pompidou's Brancusi exhibition in Paris.

n6.text: A face that lost its paint, a head that lost its body, and an island story it does not share. Today it stands in Room 170, on Floor −1 of the Denon wing.

lessons.takeaway: A marble head from the Cyclades, made around 2600–2400 BC: its makers carved only the nose and painted the rest, and nobody knows what such figures were for.
